newsitem.title: USA: Apple South hit hard by EPS disappointment.
newsitem.headline: Apple South hit hard by EPS disappointment.

text.p: Shares in Apple South Inc are not likely to post a significant near-term rebound from lower price levels seen on Wednesday, following what some analysts refer to as the stock's "second heart attack" of the year.
The largest operator of Applebee's Neighborhood Grill & Bar restaurants stunned investors this week by warning that fiscal earnings would fall short of the $0.95 per share expected on Wall Street.
The stock plunged more than 40 percent at the start of trading and stood at 12-1/2, off 8-3/8, in early afternoon.
"You can essentially take the numbers that were out there and roll them back 10 months," said Morgan Keegan analyst Craig Weichmann.
Analysts now expect Apple South's 1996 earnings to be around $0.75 per share, with 1997 earnings approaching $1.00.
J.C. Bradford analyst Barry Stouffer, who cut his rating on the company to neutral from buy, said the impact on the stock of the earnings disappointment could last six to nine months.

"There's a credibility issue about how much faith you can have in the new outlook that's been discussed, given that the company even as of several weeks ago was telling everybody that things were looking fine," he said.

"The reaction to something like this is: Sell. So, I think some of this is certainly overdone. But, frankly, our guess this morning before the market opened was that it would trade to 14 and close at 15," Stouffer added.
He and other analysts expect a near-term "dead cat" bounce by the stock into the $14-$16 range. After that, its progress toward $20 will depend on the company's delivering improved results.
"This is the (stock's) second heart-attack this year," said Weichmann, who is maintaining a moderate buy rating on the stock. "This one is major. The other one was minor."
In July the stock fell from the mid- to upper-20s to the high teens on news that then-president Michael Evans was resigning. It began edging back up in mid-August.

Analysts say Apple South's earnings growth potential, which historically has been around 30 percent a year, has been undermined by a culture clash in the Applebee stores acquired last year with the purchase of Chicago-based Marcus Group.
"They lost all of the multi-unit supervisers up there and a large number of the general managers, which means you're going to lose a large number of the employees," said Stouffer.
The response was to reinforce the Midwestern operations with seasoned managers from other parts of the country. But analysts say this only weakened the Applebee division systemwide.
The company was also hurt by the Atlanta Olympics and two destructive hurricanes.

According to Weichmann, Apple South executives have taken steps to rebuild the labor pool in hopes that better customer service will drive up revenues. The move could cost the Applebee division "a couple hundred basis points" in margin, he said, depending on how successful the effort is.
Analysts say they have been told by Apple South executives that Applebee restaurants have seen dramatic upswings in revenue at sites where improvements have been made.
Weichmann said Apple South estimates that it could derive another $80 million in revenues from about 200 Applebee restaurants, or about $400,000 per restaurant.
